# 2.9 - How Chatbots Work {.unnumbered}

In Lesson 1.6, you learned that a chatbot writes **one word at a time**. It predicts the next word, again and again.

But how does it choose the next word? Today, you build the simplest chatbot possible. It does only one thing: it **counts** which word comes next. Then it writes. You will be surprised what counting can do, and what it cannot.

{{< warmup >}}

Finish each sentence with **one word**. Do not think too long!

1. Peanut butter and ...
2. Once upon a ...
3. I am going to the ...

Compare with a partner. Which ones did you both answer the same?

:::{.think title="Why did you agree on some and not others?"}
You have read "peanut butter and **jelly**" and "once upon a **time**" many times. Your brain counted! When one next word is very common, everyone predicts it.

"I am going to the ..." has many good answers: store, park, school, bathroom. There is no single winner.
:::

{{< learn >}}

### 2.9.1 - Count What Comes Next

Here is a very small training text:

> I like rice. I like soccer. I like rice and beans. My friend likes soccer. My friend likes rice.

The tiny chatbot reads it and makes a table. For each word, it counts the words that come right after it:

| After this word ... | ... these words came next |
|---|---|
| I | like (3 times) |
| like | rice (2), soccer (1) |
| likes | soccer (1), rice (1) |
| rice | end of sentence (2), and (1) |

To write, it starts with a word and looks it up. Then it picks a next word, looks **that** word up, and so on.

:::{.real-world title="A new sentence!"}
Start with **My**: My → friend → likes → rice → and → beans → end.

**"My friend likes rice and beans."** That sentence is **not** in the training text! The chatbot made something new by mixing pieces it had seen.
:::

***

### 2.9.2 - From Counting to ChatGPT

A real chatbot has the same goal: predict the next word. But it is much, much bigger.

| | The tiny chatbot | A real chatbot |
|---|---|---|
| **Looks back at** | 1 word | thousands of words (with **attention**, Lesson 1.6) |
| **Learned from** | 5 sentences | a huge amount of text: books, websites, and more |
| **Reads text as** | whole words | **{{< glink slug="token" text="tokens" >}}**: words and pieces of words, like "play" + "ing" |
| **Picks the next word by** | counting | predicting, with a little chance mixed in |

:::{.remember}
Both chatbots predict the next word. **Neither one checks if a sentence is true.** A sentence can sound perfect and still be wrong. (You will catch this in Unit 4.)
:::

{{< tryit >}}

### 2.9.3 - The Dice Chatbot

You are the chatbot. Work in a group of 2 to 4 (or alone).

:::{.steps}
1. Finish the count table on your sheet for the training text above.
2. Start with **I** or **My**.
3. Look up the word. If there is only one next word, write it.
4. If there are two or more choices, **roll a die**. Your sheet shows which numbers go with which word. (More common words get more numbers.)
5. Keep going until you reach the end of the sentence. Write 3 sentences.
6. Did you write a sentence that is **not** in the training text?
:::

{{< talk >}}

The tiny chatbot wrote "My friend likes rice and beans." Did it **understand** that sentence? Think back to the Klingon Room in Lesson 1.3.

:::{.frames}
- The tiny chatbot **did** / **did not** understand, because ...
- A real chatbot is like the tiny chatbot because ...
- A real chatbot is different from the tiny chatbot because ...
- If a chatbot learned from text with mistakes in it, it would ...
:::

{{< further >}}

:::{.project title="Day 2: The Word-Counting Chatbot"}
This chatbot does what you did with the dice, on screen. Work with a partner.

1. Press **Learn from this text**. Click some words. Do the counts match your table?
2. Choose **always pick the most common next word**. Write a sentence. Write it again. Is it always the same?
3. Choose **pick by chance**. Write 5 sentences. Are they different?
4. Choose **a story about school**. Write some sentences. Do any of them sound strange?
5. Choose **my own text**. Write 5 sentences in **your home language**. Press **Learn**. Can it write in your language?
:::

{{< include /assets/Unit_2/word_chatbot.html >}}

:::{.think title="Why do real chatbots mix in a little chance?"}
If a chatbot always picks the most common word, it writes the same thing every time. It can get stuck saying ordinary, boring sentences.

A little chance makes the writing more interesting. Too much chance makes it strange. Chatbot makers pick a setting in between.
:::

:::{.think title="Could the tiny chatbot write in your language?"}
Yes! It does not know any language. It only counts. So it works for any language that puts spaces between words.

But it can only write words that were in its training text. A real chatbot that read very little text in your language will write it less well. (You will test this in Unit 3.)
:::

:::{.project title="Two Words Back"}
Make a new table that looks at the **last two words**, not just one. For example: after "I like," what comes next? Use it to write sentences. Are they better or worse? Why?
:::

:::{.project title="The Class Story Chatbot"}
Everyone writes 2 sentences about our school. Put them all in the word-counting chatbot. Write 10 sentences. Pick the funniest one and the most "real" one.
:::
